meta.title: Interpreting chest X-rays via CNNs that exploit hierarchical disease dependencies and uncertainty labels
meta.institution: Medical Imaging Group, Vingroup Big Data Institute (VinBDI), 458 Minh Khai street, Hai Ba Trung, Hanoi, Vietnam

headline_results.beats_radiologists: 2.6 out of 3 on hidden test set

meta.relevance_to_our_paper: Primary prior work to distinguish. Their hierarchy is at TRAINING TIME (conditional training = filter training set by parent-positive). Ours is at INFERENCE TIME (MC-Dropout variance gate). Also: their inference uses Bayes product to reconstruct unconditional probabilities; ours uses uncertainty threshold to switch prediction level.

critical_corrections_vs_prior_json: Published in Neurocomputing vol. 437, 2021 — NOT just a preprint
All 5 authors must be cited: Pham, Le, Tran, Ngo, Nguyen (VinBDI Vietnam)
14 labels are exactly enumerated in §3.1 — listed below under section 3.1
Hierarchy is the CheXpert-defined DAG from Irvin et al. [21] — NOT an invented hierarchy
Two-phase training: Phase 1 = 5 epochs on PARENT-POSITIVE subset; Phase 2 = freeze all except last FC + 5 epochs on FULL data
LR schedule: initial 1e-4, reduced by factor 10 EACH EPOCH (aggressive, not cosine annealing)
Image preprocessing: resize to 256x256 THEN template matching to find 224x224 crop — NOT just resize to 224
LSR references: Müller et al. [20] 'When does label smoothing help?' (NeurIPS 2019) AND Pereyra et al. [44]
TTA = 10 random image augmentations per test image (average outputs) — NOT Monte Carlo Dropout
Ensemble = 6 architectures: DenseNet-121/169/201, Inception-ResNet-v2, Xception, NASNetLarge
Validation set: 200 studies annotated by 3 board-certified radiologists (majority vote)
Test set: 500 studies labeled by 8 radiologists (3 as benchmark, majority of 5 = ground truth)

The Bayes product inference is the theoretical justification but after Phase 2 the model outputs are already ~unconditional — the paper notes the product is NOT applied to validation because Phase 2 uses full data

sections.title: Introduction
sections.purpose: Clinical motivation → survey of existing approaches → identify two specific gaps → contributions → road map

verbatim_key_claims: CXR: most common radiological exam for diagnosing lung and heart diseases — millions/year [1,2]
Pneumothorax [3] can be deadly if not diagnosed quickly
CAD system for most common observations from CXR will significantly benefit clinical practice
Multi-label classification for CXRs using deep CNNs = the research problem

subsections.role: Survey of prior CXR DL approaches
verbatim_key_claims: Rajpurkar [10]: CheXNet (DenseNet-121) beats pneumonia radiologist on ChestX-ray14
Rajpurkar [12]: CheXNeXt — improved DenseNet on par with radiologists on 10 pathologies
Yao [34]: CNN encoder + RNN decoder to learn label dependencies from data
Kumar [13]: cascaded DNN for multi-label classification

subsections.role: Gap identification — two specific open problems
verbatim_key_claims: Gap 1: standard multi-label classifiers often IGNORE DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE
Gap 1 specifics: how to leverage clinical taxonomies of disease patterns is an open question
Gap 2: how to handle uncertainty labels is still an open question — not received much research attention
Prior uncertain handling (U-Ignore/U-Ones/U-Zeros) are all suboptimal
subsections.writing_note: Two gaps stated in same paragraph, not separately. This is efficient for a journal intro. Our paper should state our two gaps analogously: (1) flat classifiers ignore IS-A hierarchy at inference, (2) uncertainty is quantified but not used for decision-routing.

verbatim_key_claims: Develop approach combining conditional training [19] and label smoothing [20] into novel training procedure
Adapt Chen et al. [19] conditional training to CheXpert hierarchy (different from PLCO)
Directly exploit predefined hierarchy instead of learning it from data [34]
Unlike [19][34]: also propose LSR to leverage uncertainty labels
1. Novel training strategy: (a) conditional training based on predefined hierarchy; (b) LSR for uncertain labels. Ablation verifies each independently.
2. Train series of state-of-the-art CNNs on frontal CheXpert for 14 thoracic diseases
3. Best model (ensemble): AUC 0.940 on validation; AUC 0.930 on hidden test — outperforms 2.6/3 radiologists
Section 2: related work; Section 3: proposed method; Section 4: experiments; Section 5: discussion; Section 6: conclusion

sections.title: Proposed Method
sections.purpose: Problem formulation → conditional training mechanism → LSR for uncertain labels

subsections.title: Problem Formulation
verbatim_key_claims: y ∈ {0, 1, -1}^14 where 0=negative, 1=positive, -1=uncertain
During training: apply various approaches to replace -1 with positive, negative, or smoothed
Output: ŷ ∈ [0,1]^14 via sigmoid activation on 14 logits [Eq.1]
Loss: standard BCE over all labels [Eq.2]
Evaluation: AUC on 5 pathologies (Atelectasis, Cardiomegaly, Consolidation, Edema, Pleural Effusion) — selected for clinical importance and prevalence

equations.bce: L(θ) = Σ_i Σ_k [ y_k^(i) log(ŷ_k^(i)) + (1 - y_k^(i)) log(1 - ŷ_k^(i)) ]   [Eq.2]

subsections.writing_note: Problem formulation defines all symbols used in §3.2-3.3. Notice: no masking term in the BCE — uncertain labels are resolved BEFORE computing loss (via U-Ignore/Ones/Zeros/LSR policies), unlike our project which uses explicit NaN masking.

subsections.title: Conditional Training to Learn Dependencies Among Labels

hierarchy.source: CheXpert label hierarchy proposed by Irvin et al. [21] — NOT Pham's invention
hierarchy.fig2_example: Train CNN to classify Edema, Atelectasis, Pneumonia on examples where BOTH Lung Opacity AND Consolidation are positive

verbatim_key_claims: Labels organized as tree/DAG — constructed by domain experts (radiologists), NOT learned from data
Flat classifiers fail: leaf nodes have very few positive samples → biased toward negative class
PHASE 1 (conditional training): pretrain CNN on PARTIAL TRAINING SET where ALL parent labels are positive
→ Network learns conditional probability of child labels given parent is positive
→ Duration: 5 epochs on parent-positive subset
PHASE 2 (transfer learning): freeze ALL layers except last FC; retrain 5 epochs on FULL dataset
→ Improves capacity to predict PARENT-level labels (which can be positive or negative)
Inference strategy: compute UNCONDITIONAL probability via Bayes product along root-to-leaf path
Theoretical: p(C) = p(A) × p(B|A) × p(C|B,A)  [Eqs.3-6]
Key property: p(child) is always ≤ p(parent) — clinically consistent by construction

important_nuance.about_inference: After Phase 2, the model is retrained on full data, so outputs ≈ unconditional probabilities. The Bayes product correction is the THEORETICAL JUSTIFICATION but in practice Phase 2 finetuning absorbs this. Paper states: 'this strategy is not applied to the validation set since the classifier has been trained on the full dataset during the second phase.'
important_nuance.implication: In their actual experiments, they likely use the raw Phase-2 outputs at inference, not the explicit Bayes product. The product formula guarantees p(child) ≤ p(parent) as a theoretical property.

figures.Fig1: CheXpert disease hierarchy (14 labels as tree) — relationships proposed by Irvin et al.
figures.Fig2_left: Abstract conditional training illustration: red nodes (Parent=+), blue nodes (Leaf=+/-)
figures.Fig2_right: CXR-specific example: classify {Edema, Atelectasis, Pneumonia} given {Lung Opacity=+, Consolidation=+}
figures.Fig3: 4-disease tree A,B,C,D for Bayes product derivation

equations.bayes_product_C: p(C) = p(C, B, A) = p(A) × p(B|A) × p(C|B,A)   [Eqs.3-4]
equations.bayes_product_D: p(D) = p(D, B, A) = p(A) × p(B|A) × p(D|B,A)   [Eqs.5-6]

critical_difference_from_our_paper.their_approach: Hierarchy enforced by TRAINING DATA SELECTION: exclude parent-negative samples from Phase 1
critical_difference_from_our_paper.our_approach: Hierarchy enforced by INFERENCE-TIME GATE: use MC-Dropout variance to decide whether to report child or fall back to parent
critical_difference_from_our_paper.their_uncertainty_handling: None at inference — just threshold sigmoid outputs
critical_difference_from_our_paper.our_uncertainty_handling: Explicit sigma_c > tau_u gate: high variance → suppress child → report parent

subsections.title: Leveraging Uncertainty in CXRs with Label Smoothing Regularization
verbatim_key_claims: Problem: many CXR images have uncertain labels (-1) from NLP labeler ambiguities
Prior uncertain handling: U-Ignore (wastes data), U-Ones (map -1→1, wrong labels), U-Zeros (map -1→0, wrong labels)
U-Ignore can't use full label list on whole dataset; U-Ones/U-Zeros introduce wrong labels
Propose LSR for uncertain samples: soft labels near 1 or near 0 instead of hard 0/1
U-Ones+LSR: map each -1 → u ~ Uniform(0.55, 0.85)  [soft positive] [Eq.7]
U-Zeros+LSR: map each -1 → u ~ Uniform(0, 0.3)  [soft negative]
Prevents model from being OVERCONFIDENT on uncertain training examples
LSR interval bounds [0.55, 0.85] and [0, 0.3] chosen EMPIRICALLY

equations.lsr: ỹ_k^(i) = u ~ U(a1, b1)  if y_k^(i) = -1,  else  y_k^(i)   [Eq.7]

lsr_references: [20] Müller, Kornblith, Hinton: 'When does label smoothing help?' NeurIPS 2019
[43] Szegedy et al.: 'Rethinking the Inception architecture' CVPR 2016 (introduced label smoothing)
[44] Pereyra et al.: 'Regularizing neural networks by penalizing confident output distributions' arXiv 2017
subsections.writing_note: LSR connects label smoothing (regularization technique) to uncertainty handling in multi-label CXR. The key insight: 'don't hard-commit to 0 or 1 for ambiguous labels.' Our project uses NaN masking (not-applicable) instead — a different strategy that avoids providing any supervision signal on uncertain labels.

sections.title: Experiments
sections.purpose: Dataset → preprocessing → architecture+training details → ablation → ensembling → quantitative results → radiologist comparison

subsections.title: CXR Dataset and Settings
verbatim_key_claims: CheXpert dataset: 224,316 X-ray scans from 65,240 patients
14 observations (12 common thoracic pathologies + 2 other observations)
Labels: {positive=1, negative=0, uncertain=-1} per NLP labeler
Split: Train=223,414 / Validation=200 (3 board-certified radiologists, majority vote) / Test=500 (hidden, 8 radiologists)
Test ground truth: majority vote of 5 radiologists; 3 remaining used as performance benchmarks
Evaluation: AUC on 5 pathologies (Atelectasis, Cardiomegaly, Consolidation, Edema, Pleural Effusion) — selected for clinical importance and prevalence

subsections.title: Data Cleaning and Normalization
verbatim_key_claims: Raw CXRs may have: irrelevant noisy areas (text, irregular borders), poor alignment
Preprocessing steps to reduce irrelevant factors and focus on lung area:
Step 1: Rescale all CXRs to 256×256 pixels
Step 2: Template matching [45=Brunelli 2009] → find 224×224 pixel template chest image in original
Step 3: Normalize with ImageNet training set mean and standard deviation [31=Krizhevsky 2012]
Goal: reduce source-dependent variation across CXR acquisition systems
subsections.writing_note: Their preprocessing uses template matching to CROP the lung region — this is more sophisticated than standard center crop. Our project uses center crop (224×224 after resize). Note: they normalize with ImageNet stats even though DenseNet-121 is ImageNet pretrained, so this is appropriate.

subsections.title: Network Architecture and Training Methodology
verbatim_key_claims: Backbone: DenseNet-121 [25] (ImageNet pretrained [47])
Head: 14-dim dense layer + sigmoid activations → probability of each pathology
Optimizer: Adam [46] with β1=0.9, β2=0.999, batch size=32
LR: initial 1e-4, REDUCED BY FACTOR 10 AFTER EACH EPOCH during training
Phase 1 (conditional training): 5 epochs on PARENT-POSITIVE SUBSET (excludes samples with negative parent labels)
Phase 2 (transfer learning): add back excluded samples to full dataset; freeze all layers EXCEPT last FC; train 5 more epochs on full data
Goal of Phase 2: improve parent-level label prediction (parent can be positive or negative in full data)
10 ablation conditions trained: U-Ignore / U-Ones / U-Zeros × {baseline, +CT, +LSR, +CT+LSR}
LSR intervals: U-Ones → Uniform(0.55, 0.85); U-Zeros → Uniform(0, 0.3)
subsections.hardware_framework: Keras/TensorFlow, Windows 10, single NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti 11GB
subsections.writing_note: LR reduction by factor 10 PER EPOCH is aggressive. By epoch 3 LR would be 1e-7. This works because they only train for 5+5 epochs total. Our project uses cosine annealing with warmup — quite different.

subsections.title: Model Ensembling
verbatim_key_claims: Single CNN hard to achieve high+consistent AUC for ALL disease labels simultaneously
AUC often varies with network architecture — motivates ensemble
6 architectures evaluated: DenseNet-121, DenseNet-169, DenseNet-201 [25], Inception-ResNet-v2 [26], Xception [48], NASNetLarge [27]
Ensemble: average outputs of all 6 trained networks
TTA (test-time augmentation) [49=Simonyan/VGG reference actually seems wrong - likely a different reference]: 10 random transforms per test CXR, average outputs
TTA transforms: horizontal flip, rotate ±7°, scale ±2%, shear ±5px
Ablation: also evaluated ensemble WITHOUT TTA to isolate TTA contribution
subsections.note_on_TTA: TTA is NOT Monte Carlo Dropout. TTA = 10 random augmentations of the test image, model outputs averaged. Separate from uncertainty estimation.

subsections.title: Quantitative Results

table1_auroc_validation_5labels.description: AUC on CheXpert validation set (5 pathologies), all 10 ablation conditions
table1_auroc_validation_5labels.note: ALL penalty-based scenarios use uncertain label approach as specified
table1_auroc_validation_5labels.key_finding: Best single model: U-Ones+CT+LSR = AUC 0.894. CT alone: +0.009 (U-Ignore baseline). LSR alone: +0.014 (U-Ones baseline). CT+LSR together: +0.034 — synergistic.

table2_comparison_to_prior.description: Comparison to prior state-of-the-art on CheXpert validation (5 labels)
table2_comparison_to_prior.key_finding: Ensemble+TTA (0.940) improves by ~4.5% over best Irvin et al. baseline (0.895). Largest jump in multi-label CXR at time of writing.

table4_TTA_effect.finding: TTA adds only +0.003 — also marginal. CT+LSR are the PRIMARY drivers of improvement.

verbatim_key_claims: CT and LSR contribute independently and additively — both needed for best performance
TM and TTA both marginal (<+0.006) — main improvement comes from CT+LSR
AUC for each label VARIES with architecture → ensemble important for robustness

subsections.title: Independent Evaluation and Comparison to Radiologists
verbatim_key_claims: Test set: 500 CXRs labeled by 8 board-certified radiologists
3 used as performance benchmark (AUC computed against majority-of-5 ground truth)
Model AUC on test: 0.930 (mean over 5 pathologies) — evaluated with majority of 5 as ground truth
ROC curves plotted WITH radiologist operating points overlaid
Superiority: counted number of radiologists whose operating points lie BELOW the model ROC curve
Result: model outperforms 2.6 out of 3 radiologists on average — best on CheXpert leaderboard at time

figures.Fig4: ROC curves for 5 pathologies on validation set — Atelectasis(0.909), Cardiomegaly(0.910), Consolidation(0.957), Edema(0.958), Pleural Effusion(0.964)
figures.Fig5: Example model predictions — CXR image with bar chart of probabilities for all 14 labels (4 example images)

subsections.writing_note: Radiologist comparison section is the most impactful part of CXR papers for clinical credibility. They plot radiologist OPERATING POINTS on the model's ROC curve — a clean visual showing model superiority at every operating threshold.

subsections.title: Key Findings and Meaning
verbatim_key_claims: Empirically showed major improvement by exploiting disease dependencies AND label smoothing
CT and LSR each contribute — CT adds hierarchy awareness, LSR adds robustness to uncertainty
Difficult to obtain good AUC for ALL diseases with a single CNN — architecture matters per pathology
Ensemble of multiple DL models plays key role in boosting generalization
Our findings + recent publications [10][11][12][13]: DL can identify thoracic disease risk and assist patient screening/diagnosing/physician training

subsections.title: Limitations
verbatim_key_claims: Conditional training requires PREDEFINED hierarchy — not easy to construct, usually imperfect
Difficult to scale to DEEPER hierarchies: too many examples excluded in Phase 1
LSR hyperparameters [0.55, 0.85] and [0, 0.3] chosen HEURISTICALLY — not theoretically justified
TTA increases inference time (latency concern for clinical deployment)
SINGLE INSTITUTION: trained and evaluated on CheXpert (Stanford) — geographic variation unknown
Model uses IMAGE ONLY: no patient age, gender, medical history, multi-view input
CXR quality issues: rotated, low-res, text overlays, noise — template matching insufficient to remove all
subsections.writing_note: Limitations section in journal is explicit and honest. 7 distinct limitations listed. Conference papers rarely do this. Writing an honest limitations section builds credibility with reviewers and readers.

sections.title: Conclusion
verbatim_key_claims: Comprehensive approach for building high-precision CAD for common thoracic disease classification
Investigated: data cleaning, network design, training, ensembling
Novel training procedure: CT (disease hierarchy) + LSR (uncertain labels)
Ablation confirms both components contribute independently
Ensemble+TTA: AUC 0.940 on validation, 0.930 on test; better than 2.6/3 radiologists
Future: larger clinically labeled dataset (VinDr-CXR, from Vietnam hospitals)

structural_lessons: Two-contribution methods section: §3.2 for hierarchy (the complex part) + §3.3 for uncertainty (the simpler LSR). Structure each as: motivation → approach → formula → intuition.
Ablation table (Table 1) has 10 rows = 3 uncertainty policies × {base, +CT, +LSR, +CT+LSR}. Disciplined factorial design. Each factor isolated before combining.
SOTA comparison (Table 2) puts all Irvin et al. [21] baseline variants explicitly — shows improvement over ALL of them, not just the best.
TTA and TM both ablated separately (Tables 3-4) — shows the main gains come from CT+LSR, not preprocessing tricks.
Radiologist comparison is a 'social proof' section: plot model ROC with radiologist operating points overlaid. Count how many lie below the curve.
Figure 5 (example predictions) shows all 14 label probabilities as bar chart per image — a useful visualization format for multi-label.
Limitations section has 7 explicit bullet-length points. Each is a concrete flaw, not vague hedging.

hierarchy_mechanism.pham2020: TRAINING-TIME: filter training set to parent-positive subset (Phase 1) → finetune on full data (Phase 2). Hierarchy tells WHICH SAMPLES to train on.
hierarchy_mechanism.ours: INFERENCE-TIME: use MC-Dropout variance gate. If sigma_c > tau_u, suppress child prediction and fall back to parent. Hierarchy tells HOW TO ROUTE PREDICTIONS at test time.

uncertainty_handling_training.pham2020: LSR: replace -1 with soft label u ~ Uniform(a, b). Provides soft supervision on uncertain samples.
uncertainty_handling_training.ours: NaN masking: mask uncertain labels from loss entirely. No supervision signal on uncertain labels — avoids any risk of mislabeling direction.

uncertainty_handling_inference.pham2020: No uncertainty estimation at inference. Outputs are raw sigmoid probabilities. No abstention mechanism.
uncertainty_handling_inference.ours: Explicit uncertainty estimate per label: sigma_c from T=30 MC-Dropout passes. High sigma_c → abstain or fall back to parent.

backbone.pham2020: DenseNet-121 ImageNet pretrained. Single backbone for ablation; 6 architectures for ensemble.
backbone.ours: DenseNet-121 TorchXRayVision pretrained (densenet121-res224-all). Single backbone, no ensemble.

datasets.ours: 6 datasets pooled: NIH ChestX-ray14 + CheXpert + VinDr-CXR + VinDr-PCXR + TBX11K + COVIDx (~417K studies, 51 canonical labels).

label_space.ours: 51 Indonesian clinical canonical labels (PDPI/PNPK/KKI authority). Superset of CheXpert labels.

evaluation_metric.pham2020: AUC on 5 selected CheXpert pathologies. No selective prediction metric.
evaluation_metric.ours: AUROC + F1 + ECE + AURC (selective prediction) + hierarchical consistency rate + Grad-CAM localization.

differentiation_from_our_paper.suggested_cite_sentence: Pham et al. (2020) exploit the CheXpert disease hierarchy through a two-phase conditional training procedure: first pretraining on a parent-positive subset to learn child-level conditional probabilities, then finetuning on the full dataset. While this approach enforces hierarchical structure during training, it provides no mechanism for uncertainty-based prediction routing at inference time. By contrast, our method applies the hierarchy at inference: when MC-Dropout variance for a child label exceeds a threshold, we suppress the child prediction and fall back to its parent label, providing explicit uncertainty-aware hierarchical decision support.
